Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 39, verses 4–5:

The words of the Exalted:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a liar and ungrateful.﴾ [Az-Zumar: 3] ﴿Had Allah intended to take a son, He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He wills. Glory be to Him! He is Allah, the One, the Subduer.﴾ ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth. He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term. Unquestionably, He is the Mighty, the Forgiving.﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Had Allah intended to take a son﴾ means: taking by way of honour and adoption (ittikhadh al-tashrif wa'l-tabanni), and on this reading the meaning holds together. His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿He would have chosen from what He creates﴾ confirms this. As for taking [a son] in the known sense of procreation, it is impossible to imagine it with respect to Allah, glory be to Him, and the phrase "He would have chosen" does not make sense under it. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 92] is a expression that covers both taking offspring and taking chosen ones (asfiya'). The first is rationally understood, and the second is known from the report of the Sharia. Among what indicates that the meaning here is choosing and adoption is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from what He creates﴾, that is, from His existing beings and created things. Then the Exalted declared Himself absolutely free of everything that would not be a praise. His being described as the Subduer (al-Qahhar) without restriction is because if any human is described as having subduing power, that power is restricted to a few things, and within the scope of his power over others he is himself subdued by Allah, the Exalted, in many things.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿"in truth"﴾ means: with what is obligatory and placed in its proper place, combining all the benefits.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He wraps the night﴾ means: He makes one [part] go over the other, and from it comes the expression "kawwara al-'imama" (he wound the turban), where one part is wound over another. So the part of the day or night that lengthens comes to cover part of the other, and the other that shortens enters into the one that lengthens and is hidden within it. Thus "yukawwiru" on this reading corresponds to His saying, "yulij" (He makes enter), as its opposite. Abu 'Ubayda said: "They have one meaning," and this is from his statements that are a stating (taqrir) rather than a precise determination (tahrir).

The subjection of the sun (taskhir al-shams) means its continuance in motion and the regularity of its course in accordance with what Allah, blessed and exalted, has willed. The "specified term" (al-ajal al-musamma) may refer to the Day of Resurrection, when the structure comes apart and the motion of these heavenly bodies ceases. It may also mean the times of their return to their regular cycles: every month for the moon, and every year for the sun.

﴿He created you from a single soul; then He made from it its mate, and He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock. He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation, in three darknesses. That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion. There is no god but Him, so how are you turned away?﴾

The single soul (al-nafs al-wahidah) meant in the verse is the soul of Adam (peace be upon him), as stated by Qatadah and others. It may also be a collective noun (ism al-jins).

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿then He made from it its mate﴾ (thumma ja'ala minha zawjaha), the apparent wording requires that making the wife from the soul took place after He created the creatures from it. That is not the case, and people differed in interpreting this apparent meaning. One group said: His saying ﴿He created you from a single soul﴾ refers to the taking of the offspring from the back of Adam, and that was before Hawwa' (Eve) was created from him. Another group said: "thumma" (then) here is for the sequence of reports, not the sequence of meanings. It is as if He, Exalted is He, said: "Then there had been, before that, His command that He make from it its mate." In a similar sense the following verse is recited:

Say to the one who became chief, and then his father became chief,
and before that his grandfather had already become chief.

Another group said: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿He created you from a single soul﴾ is an expression for the prior occurrence of that in Allah's knowledge. Since that was a definite matter that must occur, it was fitting to report that state which was established, and then to join to it the state of making the wife from it. So the meanings came in sequence, although the emergence of the creation of the world from Adam into existence comes only after that.

The "wife of Adam" is Hawwa' (peace be upon them both). It is said she was created from his short rib, as has been narrated. This is supported by the hadith in which the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed woman was created from a crooked rib; if you try to straighten it, you will break it." Another group said: Hawwa' was created from the same clay as Adam (peace be upon him). The first view is more sound, and its explanation has already been given.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and He sent down for you﴾ (wa anzala lakum). It was said: its meaning is that the first created of these livestock was created in the heavens and then sent down to the earth. Another group said: rather, when the command to create them and bring them into being came down from Allah, and it was customary in regard to the blessings of Allah, His mercy, His rains and other things, to say that they come from the sky, He expressed this with "anzala" (sent down). Another group said: since the rains descend, and the herbs and plants come from them, and these livestock come from the plants in their characteristics and meanings, He said "anzala" concerning them, and so it is by gradation, as the rajiz (rajaz poet) said:

The humps of the camels in its clouds.

And as the poet said:

The dew rose upon its back and poured down.

He made them eight (pairs) because each of them has a mate of the male of its kind, and they are: the sheep, the goats, the cattle and the camels.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation﴾. Ibn Zayd said its meaning is: He creates you in the wombs, creation after another creation, in the back of Adam and in the loins of the fathers. Mujahid, Ikrimah and al-Suddi said: He creates you in the wombs in stages, creation after creation, through the lump of flesh (mudghah), the clinging clot ('alaqah) and other stages.

Isa ibn Umar and Talhah ibn Musarrif recited "yakhluqukum" with idgham (assimilation) of the qaf into the kaf throughout the Qur'an. The majority recited ﴿"ummahatikum"﴾ with a damma on the hamza, while Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with a kasra; both are dialectal forms.

His saying ﴿in three darknesses﴾ (fi zulumatin thalath). One group said: the first is the back of the father, then the womb of the mother, then the placenta (al-mashimah) in the belly. Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: they are the placenta, the womb and the belly. All these signs are a lesson and an admonition for them concerning the Creator, the Fashioner, who alone deserves worship, and all of this is in refutation of the matter of the idols and of those who associate them with Allah.

Then He, Exalted is He, said to them: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾, and proofs have been established for that and the evidences have come together. ﴿So how are you turned away?﴾ That is: from what direction are you led astray, and by what cause?

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 39, verse 7:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is Free of need of you. And He does not approve disbelief for His servants. And if you are grateful, He approves it for you. And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you about what you used to do. Indeed, He is Knowing of the contents of the breasts.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: This verse addresses the disbelievers whose hearts Allah did not intend to purify. (p-375) "His servants" are the believers. It is also possible that it addresses all people, because Allah the Exalted is Free of need of all people, while they are in need of Him. By His saying, ﴿If you disbelieve﴾, He showed the distance of mankind from the pleasure of Allah if they disbelieve.

The interpreters among the People of the Sunnah differed in interpreting His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He does not approve disbelief for His servants﴾. One group said: "approval" (ridha) means "will" (irada), and the wording's apparent meaning is general but its intended meaning is specific, referring to those for whom Allah has decreed. So "His servants," on this reading, are His angels, the believers among humans and jinn, and this rests on the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Another group said: the statement is a sound general statement, and disbelief occurs from whoever it occurs from by the will of Allah the Exalted; however, after it occurs He does not approve it as a religion for them. This rests on the possibility mentioned just above. The meaning of "does not approve" is: He does not thank them for it and does not reward them with good for it. So "approval," on this reading, is an attribute of act, in the sense of acceptance and the like. Consider the difference between will and approval: the reality of will concerns what has not yet occurred, while the reality of approval concerns what has already occurred. Reflect on this in the verses of the Qur'an and you will find it, although the Arabs may use it in their poetry figuratively, one in place of the other.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if you are grateful, He approves it for you﴾ is general, and true gratitude includes faith within it. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "yarduhu" with a full (ishba') long damma on the ha'. Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read it with a short (mukhtalasa) damma. It is reported differently from Nafi' and Abu 'Amr, in the narration of Abu Bakr, as [yarduhu] with the ha' sukun. Abu Hatim said: this is an error and is not permissible.

He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾, meaning: no one will carry the sin of another. He made "bearer" (wazira) and "other" (ukhra) feminine because He intended souls (anfus). "Wizr" means weight. This is a report whose implication is an exhortation that each person look into his own particular affair and what befalls him in his own self.

Then Allah, the Exalted, informed them that their return in the Hereafter is to their Lord, that is, to His reward or His punishment, and He will make each person account for his deeds, because He is the One who has knowledge of the intentions of breasts and all other hearts. "Dhat al-sadr" (the contents of the breast) is what is hidden within it of secrets; from it is the saying of the Arabs: "The wolf is envied for its belly's owner" (al-dhi'b maghbut bi-dhi batnihi).

(p-376) The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance. Then when He bestows upon him a favour from Himself, he forgets what he was calling upon Him for before, and sets up rivals to God, to lead others astray from His way. Say: "Enjoy your disbelief for a little while; indeed, you are among the companions of the Fire."﴾

"Man" (al-insan) in this verse is intended to mean the disbeliever, as indicated by what He describes him with at the end, namely taking rivals to God, the Blessed and Exalted, and by His saying: ﴿Enjoy your disbelief﴾.

This is a verse in which God Almighty makes clear to the disbelievers that in times of hardship they always turn to Him, even though that is not from certainty or faith on their part, and therefore it is not counted for them. "Munīban" (turning in repentance) means: approaching, returning with one's insight.

God's saying ﴿Then when He bestows upon him a favour﴾ may mean: after the removal of the aforementioned harm, or it may mean any favour whatsoever, and the wording encompasses both. "Khawwalahu" (bestows upon him) means: He makes him possessor of it and gives him authority over it, beginning it from Himself, not as a recompense. One does not say khawwala of recompense (jaza'). From this comes al-khawal (servants, attendants), and from it the line of Zuhayr:

"There, if they are given wealth, they bestow it [in turn]."

(p-377) This is the transmitted reading; it is also narrated as: yustakhbalū.

God's saying ﴿he forgets what he was calling upon Him for before﴾. One group said: "ma" is a verbal-masdar particle (ma masdariyya), and the meaning is: he forgot his supplication to Him in the state of harm and returned to his disbelief. Another group said: "ma" means "alladhi" (which), and what is meant by it is God, glory be to Him and exalted; this is like His saying: ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 3], and "ma" is often used in place of "man" in countless instances of their speech. It is also possible that "ma" is a negation particle, and His saying ﴿forgets﴾ is a complete sentence; then He negates that this disbeliever's supplication was sincerely for God and intended for Him before the favour, i.e., in the state of harm. It is also possible that "ma" is a negation particle and His saying ﴿before﴾ means: before the harm; as if He were saying: this disbeliever did not used to supplicate during his whole life before the harm, but his harm compelled him to supplicate.

"Al-andad" (rivals): the opposites that oppose, contend with, and contradict one another. Qatada said: what is meant is men whom they obey in disobedience to God, the Exalted. Others said: what is meant is the idols. The majority read ﴿li-yudilla﴾ with a dammah on the yā', while Abu 'Amr, 'Isa, Ibn Kathir, and Shibl read it with a fathah on the yā'.

Then God Almighty commanded His Prophet to say to them, by way of threat, a statement addressed to one of them: ﴿Enjoy your disbelief﴾, i.e., take pleasure in it, and do what you wish "for a little while", which is the lifespan of this addressed person. Then He informed him that he is among the companions of the Fire, i.e., among its inhabitants and those who abide in it forever.

[p-378] The Exalted's words:

﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord? Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know? Only people of understanding take heed.﴾ ﴿Say: O My servants who believe, fear your Lord. For those who do good in this world is good, and God's earth is spacious. Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without reckoning.﴾

Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Hamza read "amman" with the mim lightened (takhfif). This is the reading of the people of Makkah, and also of al-A'mash, 'Isa, Shayba ibn Nassah, and it is transmitted from al-Hasan. al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim considered it weak. 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Qatada and Abu Ja'far read "amman" with the mim doubled (tashdid).

As for the first reading (with the light mim), it has two possibilities. The first, and the more apparent, is that the alif is an interrogative of affirmation (taqrir) and question. It is as if He said: "Is this devoutly obedient one better, or this mentioned one who enjoys his disbelief for a little while, and who is among the companions of the Fire?" The speech contains an elision (hadhf) indicated by the context of the verses, together with His later words: ﴿Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾. A parallel to this is the words of the poet:

"By oath, if any thing had come to us from His messenger
Other than you, but we did not find for you a repeller."

On this interpretation, the pause (waqf) falls at His words: "hoping for the mercy of his Lord."

The second possibility is that the alif is a vocative (nida'), and the address is to the people of these attributes, as if He says, "O possessor of these attributes: Say, are they equal?" Then this question with "hal" (is/are...?) is directed to the devoutly obedient one. On this interpretation there is no pause at His words, "and hoping for the mercy of his Lord."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This meaning is correct, but it is foreign to the meaning of the verses before and after it. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi considered it weak. Makki said that it is not permissible according to Sibawayh, because the vocative particle does not drop before an indefinite (mubham). It is not as Makki said. As for Sibawayh's position that the vocative particle does not drop before an indefinite, that is true, since much confusion would result from that. But as for the claim that the vocative particle has been dropped in this place, there is no such thing, and the alif here is not clearly present.

As for the second reading, "am" has entered upon "man", and the speech on this reading admits only an equation (mu'adala) between two categories. It is possible that what is equated with "am" is placed earlier in the underlying sense, as if He says: "Is this disbeliever better, or the one who...?" It is also possible that "am" has been introduced after an implied change of direction (idrab), and the equated element comes at the end of the speech. The first is clearer.

"Al-qanit" (the devoutly obedient) means the obedient one. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, explained it this way. Qunut in speech applies to recitation, and to prolonged standing in prayer. Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with him and his father, explained it this way. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Whoever wishes that God make the standing on the Day of Resurrection easy for him, let him glorify God in the darkness of the night, prostrating or standing." Qunut also applies to supplication, and to silence as an act of worship. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "qunut is obedience." Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked: Which prayer is best? He said: 'Prolonged qunut.'"

"Al-ana'" (the hours) means the periods of time. Its singular is "ina," like "mi'an" (a vessel). From it comes their saying: "Nothing will exceed its ina." From it is also His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿not waiting for its ripeness (inahu)﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53], according to some interpretations of that. It is also said of its singular "ana," on the pattern of "qafa," and it is said "inyun," with a kasra on the hamza and sukun on the nun. From this the Hudhali said:

"Sweet and bitter, like the bend of the arrow-shaft is its bitterness
In every ina that the night has passed, it puts on its shoes."

al-Dahhak read "sajid" and "qa'im" with raf' (nominative) in both.

His words, the Exalted, ﴿fearing the Hereafter﴾ mean: fearing its condition and its terror. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read: "fearing the punishment of the Hereafter." And "ulu" (possessors) means "companions," and its singular is "dhu."

The majority read ﴿Say: O My servants﴾ [al-Zumar: 53] with fath on the ya'. Abu 'Amr and 'Asim and al-A'mash made it sukun. Abu 'Amr, 'Asim also, al-A'mash and Ibn Kathir read "ya 'ibad" without the ya' in connection.

It is narrated that this verse was revealed concerning Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, and his companions, when they resolved to emigrate to the land of Abyssinia. The grammatical logic would place ﴿in this world﴾ later, though it may be placed earlier. The first opinion is more likely, that the good is in the Hereafter. Some said that by "earth" here He means Paradise, but in this view there is arbitrariness for which there is no proof.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 39, verses 11–15:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, devoting religion exclusively to Him.﴾ ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims (submitters).﴾ ﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day.﴾ ﴿Say: It is Allah I worship, devoting my religion exclusively to Him.﴾ ﴿So worship what you will besides Him.⁠ Say: Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss.﴾

In this verse, Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to openly declare to the disbelievers what he had been commanded regarding the worship of his Lord, the Exalted. His saying, ﴿And I have been commanded to be﴾, means: I have been commanded with this which I have mentioned, so that I may be the first to submit (aslama) among the people of my era and my time. This is a blessing from Allah the Exalted upon him, and a reminder from Him to him. His saying, ﴿Indeed, I fear if I disobey﴾, is a verb conditioned by a condition, which is disobedience. It is known that he, peace be upon him, is protected from it (sinning), but it is an address to his community: its ruling encompasses them, and its threat frightens them.

His saying, ﴿Say: It is Allah I worship﴾, is an emphasis of the first meaning and an announcement of his complete compliance with the command. All of this was revealed before fighting, because these were verses of truce (muwada'at). His saying, ﴿So worship what you will besides Him﴾, is an imperative form in the manner of threat, like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Do what you will﴾ [Fussilat: 40], and the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Enjoy your disbelief for a while﴾ [Az-Zumar: 8], and this is common. ﴿Those who have lost themselves﴾ is in the position of the predicate (khabar) of "inna" (indeed). His saying, ﴿and their families﴾: it has been said: its meaning is that they lost the family that would have been theirs had they been among the people of Paradise; this is like saying: they lost themselves and their bliss, i.e., what would have been theirs. It has also been said: he meant the selves and the families that they had in the world, because they have come to be in the torment of the Fire, having no settled selves, and no replacement from the people of the world; and whoever is in Paradise has either his family or others, according to the differing views on what affects that. In any case, there is absolutely no loss with him.

(p. 387) Allah the Exalted says:

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: "The matter is repeated in it many times." "Mathani" is not declined (la yanṣarif) because it is a plural with no singular counterpart in form.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 39, verses 24–28:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿Is one who shields his face from the terrible punishment on the Day of Resurrection [like one who is safe]? And it will be said to the wrongdoers, "Taste what you used to earn."﴾ ﴿Those before them denied, and the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive.﴾ ﴿So Allah made them taste disgrace in the worldly life, but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly presented for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, that they may be reminded.﴾ ﴿An Arabic Qur'an, without any crookedness, that they may become righteous.﴾

This is a statement in the sense of wonder, and the meaning is: "Is one who shields his face from the terrible punishment [like one who dwells in comfort] in Paradise?" The commentators differed concerning His saying, ﴿shields with his face﴾. Mujahid said: he crawls upon his face in the Fire. Another group said: this is in accordance with what has been related, that the disbeliever is cast into the Fire bound, his hands tied to his feet along with his neck, and he is thrown down upon his face, so he has nothing with which to shield himself except his face. Another group said: the meaning is a description of the great intensity of the punishment that reaches them, for he shields himself with all his limbs and with his senses within them; when the punishment reaches him to this extent, it becomes clear that there is nothing beyond it. This meaning, in my view, is more eloquent, and in this context the words of the poet apply:

"He meets the swords with his face and his chest, and makes his head serve in place of a helmet."

For he only intends his great boldness toward them; he meets them with every shield, and with every part of himself, even his face and his chest. As for His saying, ﴿Taste what you used to earn﴾, its meaning is: "Experience it," and here there is an omitted element, its estimated form being: "as a recompense for what you used to earn."

Then He presented to the Quraysh the examples of the earlier nations. Then Allah informed them of what those nations received in this world of being made into ill-omened tales, and other things greater than this, together with the pain, humiliation and distress that reached their souls. Then He informed them that what has been prepared for them of the punishment of the Hereafter is greater than all of this which was in the world.

As for His saying, ﴿"Qur'an"﴾, one group said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar). Another group said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and "'Arabiyyan" is also a state. Another group said: it is in the accusative as a preparatory introduction to the state (tawṭi'a lil-ḥāl), and the state is His saying, ﴿"'Arabiyyan"﴾. He negated crookedness from it, because there is no disagreement in it, no contradiction, and no flaw in any respect. The expressions of the exegetes varied: 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the meaning is "not contradictory." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "not divergent." Mujahid said: "not ambiguous." As-Suddi said: "not created." Bakr al-Muzani said: "free from grammatical error." And "'iwaj" with a kasra on the ayn is used for matters (abstract), and with a fatha for physical things (concrete entities).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 39, verse 29–32:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Allah sets forth a parable: a man in whom are partners at odds with one another, and a man belonging wholly to one man. Are the two alike in comparison? Praise belongs to Allah; but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die.﴾ ﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord you will dispute.﴾ ﴿So who is more unjust than one who lies about Allah and denies the truth when it has come to him? Is there not in Hell a residence for the disbelievers?﴾

When Allah, the Exalted, mentioned that He had set forth for people in this Qur'an every kind of parable, in general terms, He then came with a parable concerning the most important of matters and the greatest in consequence, which is tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness). He, Exalted, likened the disbeliever and the one who worships idols and devils to a slave belonging to several men, who have bad character, harshness, and lack of forbearance. Therefore they torment that slave by being irritable at their times and by burdening him with much work, so he is always toiling. Likewise is the worshipper of idols, who believes that his harm and benefit lie with them: he is tormented in thought by them and by guarding his condition from them. Whenever he seeks to please one of them by slaughtering for it, in his supposition, he thinks about what he should do with the others, so he is always in toil and error. Likewise is the one who flatters people, who is tested by serving kings.

And He, Exalted, likened the believer in Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, alone, to a slave belonging to one man who assigns him his task; he performs it deliberately, and he has been trained by his master. The master forgives his slip and thanks him for doing his work well.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

This is an announcement of the high station of Muhammad (ﷺ) and of his Lord's choosing him. "The Book" is the Qur'an.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿"bil-haqq" (in truth)﴾ may have two meanings. One is that He intends: containing the truth in its reports and its rulings. The other is that He intends that He sent it down with what was obligatory in sending it down and with what merits that, because of what it contains of the benefit of the world and the guidance of people. It is as if this act of Allah, may He be exalted, in sending down a Book to His servant, is the establishment of a proof against them, and their own striving remains after that. So whoever is guided, it is for his own self that he acted and strove; and whoever goes astray, it is against himself that he committed it. Guidance and misguidance belong to Allah, may He be exalted, in terms of creation and origination, while for the servant there is acquisition (kasb), upon which reward or punishment falls. He informed His Prophet that he is not a manager over them nor a controller. The "wakil" is the one who stands over a matter until he completes it.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, drew attention to one of His great signs which directs the observer to the Oneness, and that this has no association with an idol: it is the state of tawaffi (taking in full). That is, whatever Allah has taken in full, that is the one who dies; and whatever He has taken in a non-complete taking, that is the one who is in sleep. Ibn Zayd said: sleep is a tawaffi, and death is a tawaffi. A group has multiplied the discussion on this verse and this meaning, distinguishing between the nafs (soul) and the ruh (spirit), and another group has also distinguished between the nafs of discernment and the nafs of imagination, and so on through other statements which are only probable opinion. Then he referred those who reflect to consider this and similar matters, for it is clear that this power is possessed by none but the One, the Self-Sufficient (al-Samad).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 39, verses 43–45:

The words of the Exalted:

﴿Or have they taken intercessors besides Allah? Say, "Even though they possess nothing and do not understand?"﴾ ﴿Say, "To Allah belongs all intercession. To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; then to Him you will be returned."﴾ ﴿And when Allah alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter shudder; but when those other than Him are mentioned, behold, they rejoice.﴾

[Am] here is disconnected from what precedes it, and it is taken as implying the interrogative alif and "bal" (rather). This is a confirmation and a rebuke. Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to make them stand before the matter, and before the fact that they are content with this, although the idols are of such-and-such a form, lacking possession and reason.

The waw in His words, ﴿"Awa law"﴾ (the "waw" in "awa law"), is a conjunctive waw (waw al-'atf) that the interrogative alif has entered upon. Whenever the interrogative alif enters upon the conjunctive waw or its fa', it produces the meaning of confirmation.

Then He commanded him to inform them that all intercession belongs entirely to Allah. "Jami'an" (entirely) is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (hal). The meaning is that Allah intercedes, and no one intercedes before His intercession except by His permission. Thus, since the intercession of others is contingent upon His permission, all intercession belongs to Him and comes from Him.

As for His words, ﴿And when Allah alone is mentioned﴾ to the end of the verse, Mujahid and others said: "It was revealed concerning the Prophet's (ﷺ) recitation of Surat al-Najm at the Ka'ba in the presence of the disbelievers. At that point Satan cast into his recitation (p-400) the words, 'Indeed, they are the high cranes (al-gharaniq al-'ula), and indeed their intercession is to be hoped for.'" The disbelievers rejoiced at this and were delighted. When Allah removed what Satan had cast, they became resentful, grew arrogant, and their souls shrank. Its meaning is that they contracted from pride, disdain, aversion and repugnance. From this is the saying of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

When the sword bites into them, they recoil, and it turns them into a stubborn, unyielding hardship.

And ﴿Those other than Him﴾ means those who worship other than Him. The expression in these verses concerning the idols is used as it is used for those who act (who have reason), since they are placed in the category of those who understand, and harm, benefit and divinity are attributed to them and also denied of them, so they are treated as those who understand. "Wahdahu" (alone) is in the accusative according to Sibawayh as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and according to al-Farra' as a circumstantial accusative (hal).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 39, verses 46–48:

The Almighty said:

﴿Say: O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You will judge between Your servants concerning that over which they used to differ.﴾ ﴿And if those who did wrong possessed whatever is on the earth entirely and the like of it with it, they would surely offer it as ransom from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection. And there will appear to them from Allah that which they had not been expecting.﴾ ﴿And there will appear to them the evils of what they earned, and there will descend upon them that which they used to mock.﴾

Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to call (people) to Him and to refer the judgment to His justice. The meaning of this command includes an acceptance (of the supplication). "Allahumma" (O Allah), according to Sibawayh, is a vocative (munada), and so it is according to the Kufans, except that he disagreed with them regarding this doubled mim. Sibawayh said: it is a substitute for the omitted vocative particle, elided for brevity, and it is an indication that something has been omitted there. The Kufans said: rather, it is a verb joined to the written form, namely "amma" (come/intend), then the hamza was dropped for lightness. So the meaning of "Allahumma" is: "O Allah, intend (us) with Your mercy and Your bounty." And "Fatir" is a vocative construct (munada mudaf), i.e., "O Originator of the heavens." "Al-ghayb" is what is hidden from humankind, and "al-shahada" is what they have witnessed.

Then Allah the Exalted informed about the evil state of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, and that what descends upon them, if they were able to ransom themselves from it with the entire worldly possessions multiplied, they would surely do so. And the saying of the Blessed and Exalted: ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah﴾ (the verse). That is: their assumptions in the world were scattered and varied according to their misguidance and imaginings regarding what they believed. So when they witness the punishment on the Day of Resurrection and their states fall short, there appears to each one the opposite of what he used to assume. Sufyan al-Thawri said: "Woe to the people of showing off (riya') because of this verse." 'Ikrima ibn 'Ammar said: Ibn al-Munkadir panicked at death, and it was said to him: "What is this?" He said: "I fear this verse."

And the saying: ﴿and there descended﴾ ("wa-haqa") means: it came down, settled, and became binding. And the saying ﴿that which they used to﴾ ("ma kanu") is according to an omitted modifier (mudaf), its estimate being: "and there descended upon them the recompense of that which they used to mock."

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾

This is an argument that binds the worshippers of idols to inconsistency in their actions. That is because they worship idols and believe in exalting them, but when a calamity draws near or a hardship befalls them, they abandon and forget them, and call upon the Creator, the Originator, the Lord of the heavens and the earth. The "man" (al-insan) in this verse is generic (lil-jins). "Khawwalnahu" means "We made him a possessor" (mallaknah). Al-Zajjaj and others said: al-takhwil is giving without recompense. "Ni'mah" (favor) here is general, encompassing everything Allah bestows upon the servant. Among it is the removal of the harm mentioned, and among it are health, security, and wealth. The reference to it in the verse is indicated by His saying: ﴿I have only been given it because of knowledge﴾, and by His saying, Exalted is He, at the end: ﴿He extends provision to whom He wills and restricts﴾, and by the mention of earning (al-kasb).

He, Exalted is He, mentioned the pronoun in His saying: ﴿"uti'tuhu"﴾, and this admits several interpretations. Among them: that by the favor He means wealth, as we have already mentioned. Among them: that the pronoun refers back to the one mentioned, since the noun "ni'mah" encompasses both the masculine and the feminine. Among them: that "ma" in His saying ﴿"innama"﴾ means "alladhi" (that which). According to the first two interpretations, "ma" is a restrictive particle (kaffah), and His saying ﴿ʿala ʿilm﴾ (on knowledge) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ʿala al-hal), with "ma" being kaffah. As for when "ma" means "alladhi," then "ʿala ʿilm" is in the position of the predicate of [inna], and indicates an omitted predicate, as if he had said: "it is on knowledge."

His saying ﴿ʿala ʿilm﴾ may be understood to mean: on knowledge from me of the ways of gain and trade and other things. This was said by Qatada. In this interpretation there is self-admiration and excessive presumption, and the like. It may also be understood to mean: on knowledge from Allah regarding me, and a matter that preceded for me, and a merit I have attained with Allah, the Exalted, such that nothing harms me with it. In this interpretation there is deception regarding Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and incapacity, and presumption against Allah, the Exalted.

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Rather, it is a trial﴾, meaning: the matter is not as he said. Rather, this heedlessness regarding it is a trial for him and a test.

Then He, Exalted is He, informed about those among the earlier disbelievers that they had said something similar to this statement, like Qarun and others, and that what they earned and their reliance on wealth did not avail them. Thus it will not avail these people either.

This is a report from Allah, Exalted is He, which He brought into existence on the day of Badr and other occasions. And "mu'jizin" means: escaping and saving themselves.

Then He, Exalted is He, affirmed in truth the matter of earning and the abundance of blessings, and said: "Do they not know that Allah is the One who extends provision to some people and restricts it for others, by His will and His prior knowledge? That is not due to anyone's shrewdness nor to his incapacity." ﴿"wa yaqdiru"﴾ means: He restricts, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Then He restricted for him his provision﴾ [al-Fajr: 16].

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 39, verse 53–55:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins. Indeed, it is He who is the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you, after which you will not be helped.﴾ ﴿And follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive.﴾

(p-403) This verse is general over all people until the Day of Resurrection, both disbeliever and believer. That is to say, the repentance of the disbeliever erases his disbelief, and the repentance of the sinner erases his sin. It has been disputed whether (the forgiveness of the one who repents) is subject to the Will (of Allah), or whether he is forgiven without fail. A group among the People of the Sunnah said: he is forgiven without fail, and this is what the apparent meanings of the Qur'an require. Another group said: the one who repents is subject to the Will (of Allah), but hope prevails concerning him, and the sinner is subject to the Will (of Allah), but fear prevails concerning him.

The exegetes differed concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse. 'Ata' ibn Yasar said: it was revealed concerning Wahshi, the slayer of Hamza. Al-Suddi, Qatada, and Ibn Abi Ishaq said: it was revealed concerning a people in Mecca who believed but did not emigrate, and Quraysh tormented them, so they succumbed to the trial; then they regretted and thought that there was no repentance for them, so it was revealed. Among them were al-Walid and Hisham ibn al-'As. This is the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and that he wrote it with his own hand to Hisham ibn al-'As, the hadith (follows). Another group said: it was revealed concerning a people of disbelief from the people of the Jahiliyya, who said: "What benefit is Islam to us, when we have committed fornication, killed people, and committed every grave sin?" So it was revealed. 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, and Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them, said: this is the most hopeful verse in the Qur'an. Thawban narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I would not love to have the world and what is in it in exchange for this verse: 'O My servants.'"

"Asrafu" means: they exceeded and transgressed the bounds. "Al-qunut" is the greatest despair. Nafi' and the majority of people read ﴿(taqnatu)﴾ with a fatha on the nun. Abu Hatim said: "It would necessarily follow that they would have to read 'min ba'di ma qanatu' with a kasra, and no one has read it so." Al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read it with a damma on the nun, and Abu 'Amr, Ibn Wathhab, and al-A'mash read it with a kasra, and these are dialects.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾ is a generality used in the sense of a specification, because shirk is not included in the verse by consensus; and it is also restricted in the case of sins to the Will (of Allah). "Jami'an" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: "Indeed Allah forgives sins, all of them, and does not mind," and Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Indeed Allah forgives sins, all of them, for whomever He wills."

His exalted saying: ﴿"Wa-anibu"﴾ means: return and incline your souls (to Him). "Al-inabah" is the return of the soul to a thing. His glorified saying: ﴿before the punishment comes upon you﴾ is a warning of the punishment of this world and the Hereafter.

His exalted saying: ﴿And follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ means that the glorious Qur'an comprises luminous beliefs, commands and prohibitions that save, promises for acts of obedience and righteousness, limits upon sins, and threats upon some of them. So the best is that a person take the path of understanding, attainment, obedience, desisting, and pardoning in matters and the like; this is better than taking the path of heedlessness and disobedience, whereby he is recompensed or falls under the threat. This meaning is what is intended by "[the best]," and the meaning is not that some parts of the Qur'an are better than others insofar as it is Qur'an; rather, all of it is best in relation to human actions and what they meet of their consequences. Al-Suddi said: the best is what Allah the Exalted commanded in His Book. "Baghtatan" means: suddenly and without appointment, and "tash'uruna" is derived from "al-shi'ar" (the inner garment/sense of perception).

The majority of reciters read ﴿بِمَفازَتِهِمْ﴾ [bimafāzatihim], in the singular noun form (ism al-jins), which is a verbal noun from al-fawz (success). Al-Suddī said: al-maqālīd means the treasuries.

This expression is not a good one. One group said: there is inversion (taqdīm and ta'khīr) in the verse, as if he said: "And it has certainly been revealed to you and to those before you: if you associate partners, your deeds will surely be lost." Another group said: the verse is on its own form, meaning: "And it has certainly been revealed to every prophet: if you associate partners, your deeds will surely be lost." "Ḥabiṭa" means: it became void and fell away. By this verse, the deeds of the apostate are rendered void, including his prayer, his pilgrimage, and other things.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 39, verses 66–68:**

His Exalted and Majestic words:

﴿Rather, worship Allah and be among the thankful.﴾ ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure, while the whole earth will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand. Glory be to Him, and high is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom Allah wills. Then it will be blown again, and behold, they will be standing, looking on.﴾

*Al-maktūbah* (the word written in the mushaf, here the word "Allah"): it is in the accusative, governed by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"fa-ʿbud"﴾ ("so worship"). His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"wa-mā qadarū Allāha ḥaqqa qadrihi"﴾ ("they did not measure Allah with His true measure") means: they did not magnify Allah with His true magnificence, nor did they describe Him with His attributes, nor did they deny of Him what does not befit Him.

People differed about the referent of the pronoun in His saying, Glory be to Him, ﴿"qadarū"﴾ ("they measured"). Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: this was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh, to whom all these verses were addressed in dialogue and as a refutation. Another group said: the verse was revealed concerning a people of the Jews, who spoke about the attributes of Allah, may He be exalted, and His majesty, so they denied them, anthropomorphized Him, and made every kind of confusion; so the verse was revealed about them. In a hadith: "A rabbi came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and sat with him. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said to him: Tell us. He said: When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will place the heavens on one finger, the earths on one finger, the mountains on one finger, the water and the trees on one finger, and all creation on one finger. Then He will shake them and say: I am the King. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ laughed until his molar teeth showed, confirming him, and then he recited this verse."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited the verse as an illustration, although it had already been revealed. His saying in the hadith, "confirming him," means that he did not say anything except what he found in the books of the Jews. However, the Prophet ﷺ rejected the meaning, because anthropomorphism is evident in it. [The Jews are known for holding this belief, and they do not know how to interpret it in a way that would render the finger an expression of power, or as a finger of a creation that He creates for that purpose; and the indefiniteness of "finger" supports this.]

Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib related that the occasion of revelation of the verse was: "A group of Jews came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: O Muhammad, this is Allah who created things; so who created Allah? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ became angry and attacked them, and then the verse was revealed." The majority of people read ﴿"qadrihi"﴾ with a sukun on the *dal*. Al-Aʿmash read it with a fatha. Abu Haywa, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, al-Hasan, and Abu Nawfal read ﴿"wa-mā qaddarū"﴾ with a shaddah on the *dal* and ﴿"ḥaqqa qadarihi"﴾ with a fatha.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"while the whole earth will be His handful"﴾, means: "in His grip." Ibn ʿUmar said something to the effect that: "The earth is in the grip of one hand, and the heavens are folded up in the other hand, because both of His hands are right hands," and he related this from the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "the earth entirely is His handful, and the heavens, and all of that is in His right hand."

ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read ﴿"maṭwiyyātin"﴾ with a kasrah on the *tā'* and tanwin, while the people read it with a *ḍammah* (﴿"maṭwiyyātun"﴾).

In every case, the right hand here, the grip, and everything else that is mentioned are expressions of power and might. Whatever occurs to the hearts beyond this is false. The view of al-Qadi that they are attributes additional to the attributes of the essence is a weak opinion. In accordance with what passes through souls that knowledge has not guarded, He, Glory be to Him and Exalted, said: ﴿"above what they associate with Him"﴾, meaning: He is transcendent above all the doubts that do not befit Him.

Then He, Exalted, mentioned the blowing of the Trumpet, by which the living of the people of this world and of the heavens will be struck down. In some hadiths, through the route of Abu Hurayrah, it is related "from the Prophet ﷺ that before this swooning there is a swooning of terror," but this verse does not include it. The word ﴿"ṣaʿiqa"﴾ (swooned) in this verse means: fell down dead. *Al-Ṣūr* (the Trumpet) means the horn, and nothing else can be imagined here. Whoever says *al-ṣuwar* is the plural of *ṣūrah* (form) is referring to the blast of resurrection. Qatadah read ﴿"wa-nufikha fi al-ṣuwar"﴾ with a fatha on the *wāw*, and it is then the plural of *ṣūrah*.

His saying, ﴿"except whom Allah wills"﴾: al-Suddi said: "He excepted Jibril, Mikail, Israfil, and the Angel of Death. Then He caused them to die after this state." This was related from Anas, from the Prophet ﷺ. It was said that He excepted the prophets. Ibn Jubayr said He excepted the martyrs. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"Then it will be blown again"﴾ refers to the blast of resurrection. It is related that "between the two blasts is forty, and Abu Hurayrah does not know whether it is forty years, or days, or months, or hours." The rest of the verse is clear.

The commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 39 (az-Zumar), verses 69–72:

(p-413) The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿And the earth shall shine with the light of its Lord, and the Book shall be placed, and the prophets and the witnesses shall be brought, and judgment shall be passed between them with truth, and they shall not be wronged.﴾ ﴿And every soul shall be paid in full for what it did, and He is most knowing of what they do.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieved shall be driven to Hell in groups, until, when they reach it, its gates are opened, and its keepers will say to them: "Did there not come to you messengers from among you, reciting to you the verses of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this your Day?" They will say: "Yes, but the word of punishment has come due against the disbelievers."﴾ ﴿It will be said: "Enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein; evil is the abode of the arrogant."﴾

"Ashraqat" means: it lit up and its light became great. It is said: "sharaqat ash-shams" when the sun rose, and "ashraqat" when it shone. Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read "wa-ushriqat" with a dammah on the hamzah and a kasrah on the ra', and this is only derived from a transitive verb. So this is taken to mean: "ashraqa al-bayt" and "ashraqahu as-sirāj" (the lamp lit up the house), so the verb is used with one form whether transitive or intransitive, like "raja'a" and "raja'tuhu," and "waqafa" and "waqaftuhu." From the transitive usage, one says: "ushriqat al-ard." And "al-ard" in this verse means: the earth that is replaced by the (other) earth known to us.

As for His words: ﴿with the light of its Lord﴾, it is the attribution of a creation to its Creator, i.e., with the light of Allah the Exalted. And "al-kitab" is the Book of the reckoning of creatures, and He made it singular as a generic noun, because each person has a separate book. A group said: "the Preserved Tablet was placed." This is anomalous, and it does not carry the meaning of warning, which is the purpose of the verse.

As for His words: ﴿and the prophets were brought﴾, meaning: they were called to bear witness against their nations. As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿"and the witnesses"﴾, it was said: it is the plural of "shahid" (witness), and what is meant is the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ, whom Allah made witnesses over mankind. As-Suddi said: "the witnesses" is the plural of "shahid" (one who is martyred) in the way of Allah. This too removes the meaning of warning. It is possible that by His words "and the witnesses" He means the prophets themselves, so it is the conjunction of an attribute with an attribute by "wa," as you say: "Zayd the generous and the intelligent came." Zayd ibn Aslam said: "the witnesses" are the guardian angels (al-hafazah).

The pronoun in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿"between them"﴾ refers to the whole world, since the verse indicates it. His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ mean: nothing of their affairs will be placed other than in its proper place.

(p-414) As for His words: ﴿and every soul shall be paid in full for what it did﴾, its meaning is: it will be recompensed in full. In this is a warning, which His words, glorified is He, make explicit: ﴿and He is most knowing of what they do﴾.

The majority read "wa-suqa" and "wa-jī'a" with a kasrah on the first letter, and al-Hasan, Ibn Wathhab, ʿAsim, and al-Aʿmash read them and their like with the ishmam of a dammah. "Zumaran" means: separate groups, its singular being "zumrah." His words, Exalted is He: "futihat" is the answer to "idha" (when), and the speech here requires that its opening occurs only after their arrival, and that their standing before its opening is a humiliation for them, just as is the state of prisons and places of punishment and torment. This is unlike His words concerning the people of Paradise: "wa-futihat," with the waw indicating that they find it already opened, like the dwellings of joy.

The majority read "[futtihat]" with a shaddah on the ta' in both places, while ʿAsim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read it with a lightened ta'; this is the reading of Talhah and al-Aʿmash. Then Glorified and Exalted is He mentioned the keepers' rebuke to them concerning the coming of the messengers. The majority read ﴿"yatikum"﴾ with the ya' from below, while al-Aʿraj read "ta'tikum" with a ta' from above. His words: ﴿"minkum"﴾ are greater in argument, meaning: messengers of your own kind, whose intentions are not difficult for you and whose speech you can understand.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿They said: "Yes"﴾ are an answer to a question that affirms what is negated, and "na'am" (yes) cannot be used here, because they would have said "na'am, he did not come to us." Thus the meaning follows: then they found no proof, except that the word of punishment came due against them, i.e., the word that requires from Allah Exalted their eternal abiding in the Fire, and it is an expression for His prior decree concerning that, which is the one in His words to Iblis: ﴿"I will surely fill Hell with you and with those among them who follow you, all together"﴾ [Sad: 85].

"Al-mathwa": the place of residence.

﴿And the earth shall shine with the light of its Lord, and the Book shall be placed, and the prophets and the witnesses shall be brought, and judgment shall be passed between them with truth, and they shall not be wronged.﴾ ﴿And every soul shall be paid in full for what it did, and He is most knowing of what they do.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieved shall be driven to Hell in groups, until, when they reach it, its gates are opened, and its keepers will say to them: "Did there not come to you messengers from among you, reciting to you the verses of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this your Day?" They will say: "Yes, but the word of punishment has come due against the disbelievers."﴾ ﴿It will be said: "Enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein; evil is the abode of the arrogant."﴾

"Ashraqat" means: it lit up and its light became great. It is said: "sharaqat ash-shams" when the sun rose, and "ashraqat" when it shone. Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read "wa-ushriqat" with a dammah on the hamzah and a kasrah on the ra', and this is only derived from a transitive verb. So this is taken to mean: "ashraqa al-bayt" and "ashraqahu as-sirāj" (the lamp lit up the house), so the verb is used with one form whether transitive or intransitive, like "raja'a" and "raja'tuhu," and "waqafa" and "waqaftuhu." From the transitive usage, one says: "ushriqat al-ard." And "al-ard" in this verse means: the earth that is replaced by the (other) earth known to us.

As for His words: ﴿with the light of its Lord﴾, it is the attribution of a creation to its Creator, i.e., with the light of Allah the Exalted. This is anomalous, and it does not carry the meaning of warning, which is the purpose of the verse.

As for His words: ﴿and the prophets were brought﴾, meaning: they were called to bear witness against their nations. As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿"and the witnesses"﴾, it was said: it is the plural of "shahid" (witness), and what is meant is the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ, whom Allah made witnesses over mankind. As-Suddi said: "the witnesses" is the plural of "shahid" (one who is martyred) in the way of Allah. This too removes the meaning of warning. It is possible that by His words "and the witnesses" He means the prophets themselves, so it is the conjunction of an attribute with an attribute by "wa," as you say: "Zayd the generous and the intelligent came." Zayd ibn Aslam said: "the witnesses" are the guardian angels (al-hafazah).

"Zumaran" means: separate groups, its singular being "zumrah." His words, Exalted is He: "futihat" is the answer to "idha" (when), and the speech here requires that its opening occurs only after their arrival, and that their standing before its opening is a humiliation for them, just as is the state of prisons and places of punishment and torment. This is unlike His words concerning the people of Paradise: "wa-futihat," with the waw indicating that they find it already opened, like the dwellings of joy.

Then Glorified and Exalted is He mentioned the keepers' rebuke to them concerning the coming of the messengers. The majority read ﴿"yatikum"﴾ with the ya' from below, while al-Aʿraj read "ta'tikum" with a ta' from above. His words: ﴿"minkum"﴾ are greater in argument, meaning: messengers of your own kind, whose intentions are not difficult for you and whose speech you can understand.

Al-Zajjaj, citing al-Mubarrad, said: the answer to "idha" is omitted, its implied meaning being, after His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"abiding therein"﴾, "they were made happy" (sa'idu).

Al-Khalil said: the answer is omitted, its implied meaning being: "until, when they came to it and its gates were opened." This is like what al-Khalil estimated in the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿So when they both submitted and he threw him down upon his forehead﴾ [al-Saffat: 103].

Likewise, the saying of Imru' al-Qays has also been estimated:

"So when we passed the courtyard of the tribe and he turned aside..."

That is: "we passed and he turned aside." A group, whom Ibn al-Anbari pointed out and whose view he considered weak, said: this is the waw of eight (waw al-thamaniyah), and this waw is omitted in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, so it is like the first one.

His saying: ﴿"Peace be upon you"﴾ is a greeting. It is possible that he means that they said to them: "Peace be upon you and security for you." And "you have done well" (tibtum) means: in deeds, belief, dwelling place and reward.

His saying, exalted is He, quoting them: ﴿"and made us inherit the earth"﴾ means the land of the Garden, as said by Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi. Inheritance here is used metaphorically, because the real meaning of inheritance is that a thing passes to a person after another person's death, whereas these people inherited only the places of the people of the Fire had they been believers. "Natabawwa'" means: we take places and dwellings.

Then He described the state of the angels around the Throne and their encircling it. Some said: the singular of "hafffin" (encircling) is "haff"; another group said: "hafffin" has no singular, because the singular cannot be "haff," since ihaff is encircling something, and this word is derived from "hifaf," which means the side. From it is the saying of the poet:

"For him are glances from the two sides of his couch, when he turns them, there is punishment and bounty."

That is: from both his sides. Another group said: [min] in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"from around the Throne"﴾ is superfluous.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the correct view is that it indicates the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"glorifying their Lord with His praise"﴾: a group said: its meaning is that their glorification comes about through the praise of Allah and His favour; another group said: their glorification is by repeating and reiterating the praise of Allah, blessed and exalted is He. Al-Tha'labi said: they take pleasure (mutaladhdhidhin), not worshipping or being obligated.

(p-417) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"And it will be said, 'Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds'"﴾ is a conclusion of the matter and a definitive statement at the point of the final judgment, meaning that this just Judge ought to be praised upon the execution of His ruling and the completion of His judgment. From this verse, ﴿"Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds"﴾ has been made the closing of gatherings and assemblies of knowledge. Qatadah said: Allah opened the creation with praise, saying: ﴿"Praise be to Allah who created the heavens and the earth"﴾ [al-An'am: 1], and concluded the Resurrection with praise in this verse.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He made ﴿"Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds"﴾ the opening of His Book, so every matter begins with it and ends with it. The praise and glorification of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, ought to come from the believer, as the poet said:

"And the last thing you are in every lying down, and the first thing you are at my awakening."

Abd ibn Humayd has narrated from Wahb, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Whoever wishes to know the decree of Allah concerning His creation, let him recite Surat al-Zumar."

The commentary on Surat al-Zumar is complete, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
